newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian cyclone alert lifted, storm stays at sea.
newsitem.headline: Australian cyclone alert lifted, storm stays at sea.

text.p: Australian weather forecasters lifted cyclone warnings along Queensland's tourist coast on Tuesday as a massive cyclone hovering off the Great Barrier Reef began to weaken.

Hundreds of holidaymakers have fled gale-force winds and high seas in the Whitsunday Islands and a U.S.-Australian military exercise involving 27,000 personnel has been confined to land-based manoeuvres.

But the Australian Bureau of Meteorology said on Tuesday that the cyclone -- in sheer size the biggest to appear along Australia's east coast for 20 years -- was beginning to decline in power as the sea beneath it cooled.
"It certainly has weakened this morning," forecaster Sue Dargie told Reuters.
"The evidence of it moving towards the coast is much weaker than in previous days...That's why we've removed (cyclone) warnings along coastal areas," Dargie said.

Dargie said the Brisbane-based bureau had been comparing its own computer models of the cyclone's likely path with models provided by meteorologists in the United States and Europe and all models suggested there was no cause for alarm.
Justin was sitting over the Coral Sea around 620 kms (385 miles) off the resort of Cairns.
An Australian military spokesman said that Tandem Thrust '97, the largest U.S.-Australian wargames since World War Two, had been hit but not derailed by the cyclone.
"At this stage, 80 percent of the exercise objectives have been achieved," the spokesman said.
The land, sea and air wargames which began on Monday and is due to end on March 22, bringing together 27,000 personnel and more than 200 warships.
The spokesman said bad weather caused by Justin had forced the delay or cancellation of some air and sea exercises. Land-based manoeuvres were proceeding on schedule.
In the Whitsundays, a group of islands on the southern tip of the Great Barrier Reef, hundreds of tourists have either called off holidays or left early as the winds and seas rose.
Terry Hudson, managing director of Whitsundays Rent-a-Yacht, said all his company's 40 boats were tied up, lashed down and prepared to ride out any possible cyclonic winds.
"We had 11 boats on charter with 35 people including two U.S. families," Hudson said. "All the boats have been recalled, are now safe and the families on shore."
Hudson said some islands had been hit by winds of over 100 kph (60 mph), the strongest winds in years.
"It's caused damage to beaches and foreshores but it's more annoying than anything else," Hudson said.
Tourism operators on the mainland said it was business as usual despite the threat from Justin, with larger islands operating normally.
"It's a beautiful day in Cairns -- very little wind and the cyclone is still a long way off the coast," said a spokesman at a luxury hotel in the resort of Cairns.
"We are not planning to do anything out of the ordinary and the guests are enjoying themselves," he said.

The winds brought on by the cyclone have interrupted exports from north Queensland's three main bulk coal ports. Sugar cane growers -- the state is Australia's main sugar producer -- were also nervously watching the cyclone's progress.
"You only need the crop to be damage and world prices will skyrocket," said one commodities broker on Tuesday.
